David Foster Wallace. The American novelist, essayist, and short-story writer who synthesized postmodern narrative difficulty with earnest engagement with consciousness, suffering, and meaning-making. His masterwork, Infinite Jest, published in 1996, is a thousand-plus-page postmodern epic that established him as a defining voice. His essays on literature, tennis, and American culture are now canonical. His voice—erudite, funny, desperate—defined a generation's confrontation with information overload, entertainment, addiction, and the search for authentic connection.

Infinite Jest remains sprawling and encyclopedic, set in a near-future North America dominated by corporate entertainment and addiction. The novel braids together tennis academies, drug rehabilitation, wheelchair-bound assassins, and the lethal power of a film so entertaining it kills viewers. He employed nested narratives, hundreds of footnotes, and a dense, maximalist prose style. The novel is formally challenging and deliberately overwrought, treating postmodern excess as both an aesthetic and thematic problem. His essay "A Supposedly Fun Thing I'll Never Do Again," about a luxury cruise, blends reportage, digression, and philosophical inquiry, as does "Consider the Lobster," on the Maine Lobster Festival. His essays are literary performances. Wallace treated postmodern irony and detachment as moral and psychological crises. His work argues for sincerity, emotion, and connection despite—or through—postmodern skepticism. The Pale King, published after his death, is an unfinished novel about IRS workers. Its fragments explore boredom, attention, and bureaucratic consciousness. His suicide in 2008 cast his work's engagement with depression, addiction, and meaninglessness as tragically prophetic. He became a symbol of postmodern disaffection and its costs. Thomas Pynchon remained his greatest literary ancestor, whom Wallace explicitly referenced and responded to. Both treated narrative difficulty as formal necessity.
